content.p: John O'Keefe, a 46-year-old Boston police officer, was found lying in the snow outside a house in Canton, Massachusetts, a little after 6 a.m. on 29 January 2022, during a blizzard. He was taken to hospital and pronounced dead. The medical examiner found that he had died of blunt force injuries to the head, with hypothermia contributing. Prosecutors charged his girlfriend, Karen Read, with second-degree murder, alleging that she had reversed her SUV into him while drunk and left him to die. She said she was being framed.

After two trials, a jury acquitted Read on 18 June 2025 of murder, manslaughter and leaving the scene of a fatal collision. It convicted her only of driving under the influence, for which she received a year of probation. No one else has been charged. The case divided the suburbs south of Boston, led to the firing of the lead investigator over his text messages, and has since moved into a series of civil lawsuits.

O'Keefe and Read had begun dating during the Covid-19 pandemic. He was caring for his niece at the time. Messages and voicemails later made public suggested the relationship was strained in the weeks before his death, and on the evening of 28 January, with a major snowstorm on the way, the couple went out with friends to two Canton bars, C.F. McCarthy's and the Waterfall Bar and Grill. Video shown at trial, prosecutors said, showed Read drinking a number of cocktails.

Shortly after midnight the group arranged to carry on at 34 Fairview Road, the home of Brian Albert, a Boston police officer. Read drove O'Keefe there. What happened in the next few minutes was the whole case. Read said she dropped him off and watched him go into the house. The people inside testified for the prosecution that he never came in. Data from her Lexus, according to a biomechanical engineer called by the prosecution, recorded the SUV moving forward 34 feet at 12:32 a.m. and then accelerating backward for 53 feet at about 24 miles per hour. An expert testified that data from O'Keefe's phone showed steps after he left the car, ending a few minutes later; the phone did not move again until morning.

At around 1 a.m., investigators said, Read left him voicemails, one of them saying, "John, I f------ hate you." A toxicologist put her likely blood alcohol content at around 12:45 a.m. at between .13 and .29, over the legal limit.

O'Keefe did not come home. At 4:23 a.m. O'Keefe's niece phoned Jennifer McCabe, a friend of his who is Brian Albert's sister-in-law, to say Read was distraught. McCabe said she heard Read screaming that John had not come home and that they had fought. Read, McCabe and a third woman went out to look for him in the storm. Prosecutors said Read mentioned a crack in her tail light and wondered aloud whether she could have hit him. A surveillance camera at O'Keefe's house had recorded her SUV at 5:07 a.m. coming "extremely close" to his car in the driveway. Prosecutors said no tail light pieces were found there; the defence said she had struck his car, and that this explained the broken light.

At about 6 a.m. the women found him in the snow near a flagpole in the Alberts' front yard. Several first responders testified that Read, hysterical, said repeatedly, "I hit him." Her lawyers said her words had been twisted into a confession that she never made.

One detail of that morning became famous. At some point someone searched Google on McCabe's phone for "hos long to die in cold". McCabe testified that Read had asked her to look it up after the body was found, and prosecutors put the search at 6:23 and 6:24 a.m. The defence said a federal forensic expert had placed it at 2:27 a.m., hours before anyone was supposed to know O'Keefe was outside. Both trials heard competing expert evidence on the timing.

That afternoon a state police team sifted the snow near where he lay and found pieces of red tail light plastic, one of O'Keefe's shoes, and the broken cocktail glass he had carried out of Read's car. Investigators took custody of the Lexus the same day, and prosecutors argued that the timing made it impossible for anyone to have planted the fragments. Prosecutors later said tail light material was found on his clothing and that DNA on the tail light matched his.

Read was first charged in February 2022 with manslaughter and related offences. In June 2022 a Norfolk County grand jury indicted her for second-degree murder, manslaughter while driving under the influence and leaving the scene. She pleaded not guilty and was released on $100,000 bail.

In 2023 her lawyers, Alan Jackson and David Yannetti, laid out a very different account. They said O'Keefe had gone into the house, been beaten in a fight and attacked by the Alberts' dog, pointing to wounds on his arm, and that his body had been put outside afterwards. They accused people in the house and members of the state police of covering it up. Albert and Higgins have denied any involvement, and prosecutors said the claims had been refuted by the evidence. District Attorney Michael Morrissey called the theory baseless and condemned what he described as harassment of witnesses. "Conspiracy theories are not evidence," he said. A blogger who often filmed himself confronting witnesses, Aidan Kearney, was arrested in October 2023 on charges of intimidating witnesses.

The prosecution's investigation had its own problem. The lead investigator, State Trooper Michael Proctor, had been brought in because Brian Albert's brother served in the Canton police. But Proctor's sister was a friend of Albert's sister-in-law, and the defence questioned his family's friendship with another Albert brother. In March 2024 the state police opened an internal investigation into him.

The trial opened in Dedham in April 2024 before Judge Beverly Cannone. Brian Albert testified that O'Keefe and Read never entered his house. Brian Higgins, a federal agent who had been at the gathering and who had exchanged flirtatious messages with Read in the preceding weeks, also testified; the defence suggested him as a possible suspect, and he denied any involvement.

The turning point was Proctor's testimony in June. He was made to read to the jury messages he had sent about Read to friends, family and fellow officers while running the investigation. He called her a "whack job", joked that he had found "no nudes so far" when searching her phone, and told his sister he hoped she would kill herself. He called the messages unprofessional and regrettable but said they had no bearing on the integrity of the investigation.

The jury deliberated over several days and twice reported that it was deadlocked. On 1 July 2024 Cannone declared a mistrial. Hours later the state police relieved Proctor of duty. Afterwards several jurors told the defence that the panel had in fact agreed unanimously to acquit on two of the three charges. Read's lawyers argued that retrying her on those counts would be double jeopardy, but the state's highest court, a federal judge and finally the US Supreme Court all declined to stop the retrial.

Morrissey brought in Hank Brennan, an experienced trial lawyer, as special prosecutor. In March 2025 Brennan confirmed in court that a federal investigation connected to the case had ended without charges, and on 19 March 2025 the state police fired Proctor. The second trial opened in April 2025. Neither side called Proctor, Albert or Higgins, and Cannone did not allow the defence to name them as alternative suspects, though it could argue that Higgins had not been properly investigated.

Brennan built his case on data and on Read's own words. He played clip after clip from television interviews she had given between the trials, in some of which she seemed to allow that her car might have touched O'Keefe, and in others denied it outright. "There is zero chance John was hit by a vehicle," she said in one. His engineer told the jury that the dozens of cuts on O'Keefe's right arm fitted the broken tail light. "She could have broken up with him," Brennan told the jury in closing. "She doesn't drive away." He told them they should be disgusted by Proctor's messages, but that "that doesn't change the physical evidence, the scientific evidence and the data."

The defence concentrated on reasonable doubt. Crash reconstruction experts said neither the damage to the Lexus nor O'Keefe's injuries fitted a collision, and a pathologist testified that his arm wounds looked like dog bites. A snowplough driver who passed the house several times in the hours after the alleged collision said he saw no one lying in the yard. Jackson asked the jury why the lead investigator had not been called. "Michael Proctor was clearly radioactive," he said. Read did not testify.

Jurors began deliberating on 13 June 2025. On the fourth day the judge briefly announced that they had reached a verdict, only for them to take it back; minutes later they delivered it. Read was acquitted of second-degree murder, of manslaughter while under the influence and of leaving the scene, and convicted of operating under the influence. Cannone sentenced her on the spot to a year's probation, the standard sentence for a first offence.

Hundreds of supporters, many dressed in pink, cheered outside. "No one has fought harder for justice for John O'Keefe than I have," Read told them. O'Keefe's family left the courtroom as the judge thanked the jurors. Witnesses who had testified for the prosecution, among them McCabe and Roberts, issued a statement calling the result "a devastating miscarriage of justice" and blaming "lies and conspiracy theories spread by Karen Read, her defense team, and some in the media." "The jury has spoken," Morrissey said. Proctor told ABC that the idea he had planted evidence was ridiculous.

In August 2024, between the trials, O'Keefe's family, led by his brother Paul, had sued Read and the two bars for wrongful death, accusing her of hitting him and the bars of over-serving her. Read's lawyers have asked to have it dismissed; it was still being fought in Plymouth Superior Court in 2026, with the judge telling the lawyers to stop pandering to social media.

Read went on the offensive too. In November 2025 she sued Proctor, McCabe, Higgins and other witnesses. In April 2026 four trial witnesses sued her and Kearney for defamation. On 4 June 2026 she sued the Massachusetts State Police and the town of Canton, claiming she had been wrongfully prosecuted. The suit reproduced messages attributed to Proctor and to a Canton police sergeant, Sean Goode, who had testified in the first trial, which, the suit said, included racial slurs. The state police chief, Colonel Geoffrey Noble, called Proctor's messages "racist, sexist and abhorrent" and said they confirmed his decision to fire him. Goode resigned in late May 2026 as Canton moved to dismiss him. Proctor's lawyer said the evidence that Read killed O'Keefe was overwhelming and that nothing in his client's personal life had any bearing on the investigation.

The prosecution has never accepted the cover-up theory. It has maintained that O'Keefe's phone data and the statements of 11 witnesses show he never entered the house, and that the medical examiner found no sign of a fight. Read's probation ended in June 2026. Who or what killed John O'Keefe has not been established by any court.
